units.passage: e recognize it is a losing battle to prevent AI use.
units.why: 'it is a losing battle to prevent AI use' states staff will not rely on preventing AI and use redesign instead, closest to P60.

units.passage: This approach removes you from evaluating whether students used AI in their work. Rather your focus is on evaluating if they met the expectations for the work or not, and being evaluated on that alone.
units.why: This approach "removes you from evaluating whether students used AI in their work", so instructors do not police AI use and assess against expectations alone (P60).

units.passage: We will not attempt to enforce this rule, as we believe that is fundamentally impossible, but you need to understand that if you break this rule, you are cheating
units.policy: We will not attempt to enforce this rule, as we believe that is fundamentally impossible, but you need to understand that if you break this rule, you are cheating
units.why: Staff say they will not enforce the ban because it is 'fundamentally impossible': declining to police AI use (P60); the unverifiable-control point (P82) is secondary.
units.fit_note: Also says enforcement is judged impossible (P82).

units.passage: This doesn’t mean that, as instructors, we should simply throw up our hands in defeat, but it does mean that we will increasingly need to trust our students to follow our policies voluntarily
units.policy: Instructors will increasingly need to trust students to follow AI policies voluntarily, since prohibitions may be unenforceable in practice.
units.why: "we will increasingly need to trust our students to follow our policies voluntarily" says instructors will rely on student good faith rather than policing: should, P60.

units.passage: Chasing after “cheating” students, particularly as technologies continue to develop additional capabilities, is a losing game
units.why: 'Chasing after "cheating" students ... is a losing game'; recommends investing in course updates not policing. P60 (decline to police).

units.passage: we recommend that faculty generally avoid actions that over-prioritize “catching/preventing cheating.”
units.why: Faculty should 'generally avoid actions that over-prioritize catching/preventing cheating'; P60 decline to police.

units.passage: Adopting intensive surveillance tools or processes — such as requiring all steps of writing to be done under human or technological supervision — is likely to produce few gains
units.why: 'Adopting intensive surveillance tools or processes ... is likely to produce few gains'; against surveillance, P60 (not policing).

units.passage: Moreover, using AI detectors shifts pedagogical focus to policing, undermining the trust between students and educators, and offers only a short-term solution as AI technology is rapidly evolving.
units.why: "using AI detectors shifts pedagogical focus to policing, undermining the trust between students and educators" is a stated reason to avoid policing: P60.
units.fit_note: Argues against detector-based policing; does not say staff decline to police.; Gives trust and pedagogy as reasons to avoid detector-based policing; does not say staff will not police.

units.passage: The goal should not be to design assessments that police student behavior . Instead, design courses so that showing up is more interesting and more rewarding than sending an agent in your place.
units.why: "The goal should not be to design assessments that police student behavior": assessments built to engage rather than police, P60 (declining to police).
units.fit_note: Says assessment design should not police; it does not say staff will not detect AI use. / It says assessment design should aim for engagement rather than policing, not that policing is refused.

units.passage: For instance, many instructors recounted that having to “police” unauthorized AI use was harming their connection to students (a dynamic made worse by the fact that, as we learned, AI detection software is quite unreliable).
units.why: Instructors 'having to "police" unauthorized AI use was harming their connection to students'; this is rationale against policing (P60, decline to police).

units.passage: More generally, stepping up “policing” around AI use builds an adversarial atmosphere of distrust between instructors and students, which understandably hurts students’ motivation and morale.
units.why: 'stepping up "policing" around AI use builds an adversarial atmosphere of distrust' states a consequence that argues against heavy policing (P60); it directs nothing itself, so informs.

units.passage: Students should not feel policed. Durable change will require instructors to be as clear as possible about their expectations and students to understand AI misuse as an unacceptable deviation from August13,2026 ReportofMIT’sAdHocCommitteeonAIUse 18 shared peer norms and community values rather than a violation of an arbitrary bureaucratic rule.
AI Literacy offers a strong alternative to policing and detection approaches.
units.why: 'AI Literacy offers a strong alternative to policing and detection approaches' recommends literacy instead of policing, the closest type being P60 (decline to police), although here it is a recommendation by the teaching center.
units.fit_note: Coder A: Recommends AI literacy as the alternative to detection; it is not staff stating they will not police. Coder B: Also recommends AI literacy as the replacement for policing, which P60 does not mention.

units.passage: Rather than police and penalize AI use, help students develop AI literacy so they are equipped to scrutinize AI outputs, recognize potential errors or bias, and consider the appropriateness of AI within their disciplines and lives.
units.policy: Rather than police and penalize AI use, help students develop AI literacy.
units.why: Principle 6 begins "Rather than police and penalize AI use", saying the approach is not to police; P60 (decline to police) because it contrasts policing with building AI literacy.
units.fit_note: Also asks instructors to teach AI literacy (scrutinizing outputs, errors, bias) as the alternative to policing.

units.passage: This isn’t about surveillance! The goal is not to “catch” AI misuse but rather to cultivate responsible and effective use.
units.why: 'This isn't about surveillance! The goal is not to "catch" AI misuse' says staff aim to cultivate responsible use rather than police it; P60 (decline to police) is the nearest fit.
units.fit_note: Does not rule out enforcement; it frames the purpose as cultivating responsible use rather than stating that no policing will occur.

units.passage: Clarity and ongoing dialogue are more effective than policing and better support our trust-based academic community.
units.why: States that dialogue is "more effective than policing"; nearest is P60 (decline to police), a partial fit because it prefers dialogue rather than saying staff will not police.
units.fit_note: Prefers clarity and dialogue to policing; does not say staff will not detect use. Frames dialogue as better than policing as a principle; does not commit staff to not policing.

units.passage: Teaching to police errors and wrongdoing simply doesn’t emphasize student growth and learning.
units.why: 'Teaching to police errors and wrongdoing simply doesn't emphasize student growth and learning' advises instructors not to focus on policing. P60 fits.
units.fit_note: Advises against a policing focus rather than saying staff will not police.
